name: bad_knight
description: Bad knight: "A knight on the rim is dim". A knight on the a- or h-file has at most 4 squares it can hop to. We flag a rim knight as "bad" when at most one of those squares is both unoccupied by a friendly piece AND not attacked by an enemy pawn — i.e., the knight has nowhere useful or safe to land.

name: bahr
description: Bahr's rule -- KPP vs KP rook-pawn endings the rule calls drawn. https://www.arves.org/arves/index.php/en/endgamestudies/theory/1570-the-flaw-in-bahr-s-rule Bahr's rule covers a pawn ending with two blocked rook pawns plus one extra "outside" passed pawn for the stronger side. The rule says the position is a DRAW (the defender holds) when all three conditions hold: 1. The stronger side's rook pawn has NOT crossed the half-way line, i.e. it is no further than its own 4th rank. If it has, the stronger side wins. 2. The stronger side's king stands next to (is adjacent to) its passed pawn. 3. The defending king stands directly in front of the passed pawn, or directly in front of the attacking king. The rule is only a guideline: F. Santelli's position 8/8/8/8/p3k3/P7/4KP2/8 meets all three conditions yet is in fact won for the stronger side when the defender is to move (the John Crum manoeuvre) -- this is the "flaw" discussed in the ARVES article above. Because the rule itself says nothing about the side to move, this query matches the geometry regardless of whose turn it is, so the rare flawed positions are matched too.

name: triangulation
description: Find king triangulation patterns. A triangulation is a king maneuver where the king moves to 3 different squares forming a triangle and returns to its starting square. Pattern: K@A -> K@B -> K@C -> K@A (3 king moves, A != B != C) We detect this at the position right after the third king move. At that position, going back through the parent chain: current (P):    K@A, just after K_C->A parent (P-1):   K@C, side-that-triangulated about to play K_C->A parent^3 (P-3): K@B, same side about to play K_B->C parent^5 (P-5): K@A, same side about to play K_A->B  [START]

name: triangulation_general
description: Find triangulation by any piece (king, queen, rook, or bishop). Pawns can't move backwards, and knights always change square color in 3 moves -> they can never triangulate. So we restrict to K, Q, R, B. We use piece tracking (piece variables preserve a piece's identity across positions even when there are multiple pieces of the same type) to follow one specific piece through 3 moves. Pattern detected at the position right after the third move: start_pos (P-5): piece on square A, side X to move P-4..P-3:        side X plays piece A->B P-2..P-1:        side X plays piece B->C current  (P):    side X plays piece C->A   <- we are here

name: unguarded_guard
description: Unguarded guard: A line-check is parried by interposing a piece on a square that is not defended by any of the defender's other pieces — the "guard" itself is unguarded. 1. parent:check, not check       -> the played move resolved a check 2. piece $checker in [rbq]       -> the checker was a sliding piece (flipcolor symmetric) 3. parent:($checker attacks K)   -> $checker was attacking the white king at parent 4. $line = parent: between(...)  -> squares strictly between checker and king at parent 5. $block = $line minus squares attacked by white at current (the interposed piece is not defended by any other white piece — a piece never attacks its own square, so the blocker itself does not appear as a defender) 6. parent: (move to $block)      -> the move played from parent landed on such a square
